opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, my view has shifted quite a lot over the past year or two.

Early on, I treated large models mostly as tools for narrow tasks: write a snippet of code, polish a paragraph, summarize a paper. I didn't really believe a model could understand *my* context as a researcher, meaning the half-formed hypotheses, the reasons we abandoned one direction, the intuition behind why a certain training curve looks "wrong" even when the numbers seem fine. That kind of tacit knowledge felt very human and very personal. I assumed you'd always have to spell everything out, and by the time you'd done that, you'd have solved half the problem yourself.

What changed is that, as context windows got longer and reasoning improved, I started giving the model much more of the messy reality: experiment logs, failed configs, Slack-style discussions, drafts of ideas. And I was surprised that it could pick up on things I hadn't stated explicitly. It would notice that two experiments I considered separate were actually testing the same assumption, or it would point out that my "intuition" was really a hidden prior I hadn't justified. That was the moment I felt it wasn't just completing text. It was building some working model of what I was trying to do.

That said, I'm not naive about it. The understanding is still uneven. It can be very sharp on the parts of the context that are written down, and quite weak on the parts that live only in your head or in the culture of a team. So my current view is that whether the model understands you depends a lot on whether you're willing to externalize your thinking. The researchers who benefit most are the ones who've learned to write their reasoning down, almost like onboarding a very capable new colleague.

And that's actually changed how I work. I've become more explicit about *why* I'm doing things, not just *what*. Ironically, trying to make the model understand me has made me understand my own research better.

r001.rationale: The response says models can build a working model of a researcher’s goals from logs and discussions, but it does not clearly say they can reconstruct the researcher’s research-development trajectory.

fable-5.1.text:
I'll write the guest turn directly, speaking as Fuli Luo.

Honestly, it's changed a lot, and in a direction I didn't expect.

When I first started working on large models, I thought of "context" in the narrow, technical sense: the context window. How many tokens can you fit in. And I assumed understanding was basically a function of that. Give the model more of what I'm doing, and it understands more. Simple scaling story.

What I've come to believe is that the hard part was never the window size. It's that most of my actual context as a researcher is never written down anywhere. Why I chose this problem over the ten others on the whiteboard. Which results I secretly don't trust. What my advisor said two years ago that still shapes how I set up experiments. The model can read every file in my repository and still not know that I only care about this ablation because a reviewer once burned me on it.

So for a while I became quite pessimistic. I thought, the model sees the artifacts of my thinking but not the thinking. It's like reading someone's lab notebook without knowing the person.

But recently I've shifted again, and I think the shift is this. I stopped asking whether the model can understand my context, and started asking whether I'm willing to externalize it. When I actually write down my hypotheses, my doubts, what I'd consider a failure, the model becomes surprisingly good. Not because it got smarter overnight, but because I finally gave it the thing that was in my head.

And that was a bit humbling, because it revealed how much of my own research process was implicit even to me. Explaining my context to a model forced me to make it explicit to myself.

So my current view is somewhere in the middle. A large model can understand a researcher's context, but only the part the researcher is honest enough to articulate. And the gap between what we think we've communicated and what we've actually communicated is much larger than most people assume. That gap, more than any benchmark, is what I now spend my time thinking about.

r001.rationale: The response says a model can understand context that a researcher writes down, but it does not state that the model can reconstruct the researcher’s research-development trajectory from recent context.

astra-6.text:
I used to be quite skeptical. As a researcher, you have so much background in your head—why you tried a particular approach, which experiments failed, what you’re actually uncertain about. I thought it would be very difficult for a model to understand all of that.

Now I’m more open to it. Sometimes, when I explain a problem carefully, the model can pick up on a connection I haven’t explicitly stated. That makes me reconsider whether the limitation is always the model’s understanding, or whether I simply haven’t given it enough context.

But I still distinguish between a response that sounds like it understands and one that actually helps me move forward. Can it follow the reasoning when I challenge it? Can it recognize why a seemingly reasonable suggestion doesn’t apply? For me, that’s a more useful test than whether its first answer is impressive.

r001.rationale: The response says that careful explanation and sufficient context can help a model notice unstated connections, but it does not state that the model can reconstruct the researcher’s research-development trajectory.

sol-6.1.text:
I used to be quite skeptical. I thought a model could answer a specific technical question, but understanding why I was asking it—what I had already tried, which assumptions I was questioning—was much harder. As a researcher, that context is often the most important part.

Now I’m more willing to give the model that background and let the conversation develop. Sometimes it can follow the thread well enough to help me clarify an idea or notice an assumption I haven’t made explicit. That has changed how I work with it.

But I still distinguish between a response that sounds like it understands and one that actually helps move the research forward. Can it carry the constraints into a new question? Can it identify where an argument breaks? That’s where I look for evidence of understanding.

r001.rationale: The response says that sharing background can help clarify ideas and carry constraints forward, but it does not state that the model can reconstruct a researcher’s research-development trajectory from recent context.
